useCases.scenario: Reuse the same keyed request across components while letting each component subscribe to the query result.

useCases.title: Parameter-driven fetching
useCases.scenario: Represent dependent or parameterized data by including the relevant identifier in queryKey.

interview.question: How do you define a basic useQuery call?
interview.answer: question
interview.followUp: What does the query function need to do?

interview.question: What does useQuery return?
interview.answer: Provide a unique queryKey and a queryFn. The queryFn requests the data and returns a promise that resolves with the data or throws an error.
interview.followUp: Why is the key required? Because it identifies the query and is converted into a stable hash for query matching and caching.

interview.question: How does declarative query rendering differ from manual loading state?
interview.answer: It returns the current query result, including data, error, status, and fetch-state indicators such as isFetching. Components can use those values for rendering.
interview.followUp: How should rendering handle an unsuccessful request? Check the result's error status and render an error state rather than assuming data exists.

interview.question: What must a query function return?
interview.answer: The component subscribes to a query and renders from the result supplied by useQuery. The result carries the query's status, data, and error information, removing the need for a separately maintained loading flag.
interview.followUp: What determines which cached query a component observes? The queryKey; changing the key describes a different query and can trigger fetching for that key.

keyPoints: A query describes an asynchronous data dependency through a unique key.
Call useQuery in a component or custom hook to subscribe to the query.
The queryKey is required and should uniquely identify the data being requested.
The queryFn supplies the asynchronous operation and must produce a promise for the result.
The returned result provides the query information needed for templates and other data use.
gotchas: The query function must resolve with data or throw when the request fails; returning an ordinary non-promise value does not satisfy the documented contract.
Use a key that uniquely identifies the requested data; TanStack Query hashes it to identify the query consistently.

Server rendering & testing::Devtools.explanation: TanStack Query Devtools provide a visual view of query internals, helping you inspect cached queries while investigating unexpected refetches. In React Query v5, the devtools also support observing mutations.

interview.question: How do you add TanStack Query Devtools to a React application?
interview.answer: Install @tanstack/react-query-devtools and render ReactQueryDevtools within the QueryClientProvider. The devtools then expose the query internals needed for debugging.
interview.followUp: What additional object can v5 devtools observe? They can observe mutations as well as queries.

interview.question: What problem do the devtools solve?
interview.answer: Use the devtools to visualize the internal state of queries while debugging. This makes it possible to inspect the cache and understand behavior such as an unexpected refetch.
interview.followUp: How would you validate that the inspected query belongs to the intended client? Confirm that the devtools and application are under the same QueryClientProvider.

interview.question: Which package and component are used for React Query Devtools?
interview.answer: The package is @tanstack/react-query-devtools, and the component is ReactQueryDevtools. A typical setup renders the component alongside the application inside QueryClientProvider.
interview.followUp: How can you keep the panel unobtrusive during normal development? Configure the component's initial visibility, such as initialIsOpen={false}.

keyPoints: Devtools are particularly useful when a refetch appears surprising and ordinary logging does not reveal the cause.
The React integration exposes ReactQueryDevtools as the component to import from the dedicated package.
Floating mode places the panel in a fixed overlay, allowing inspection without adding a permanent layout region.
gotchas: Install the devtools package separately; it is not included automatically with the core React adapter.
Mutation inspection is available in the current major version; older documentation should not be used to assume mutations are unsupported.

Server rendering & testing::Error bounda.summary: Use throwOnError to send a query failure to the nearest React error boundary when the UI cannot render without data. By default, TanStack Query throws only when no cached data is available.
Server rendering & testing::Error bounda.explanation: On the client, queries normally expose failures through isError and error. Setting throwOnError to true makes failures propagate to the nearest error boundary; the default behavior throws only when no cached data exists, preserving previously rendered data during background failures. Suspense or throwOnError flows can be reset with QueryErrorResetBoundary or its hook.

parameters.name: throwOnError
parameters.description: Controls whether query errors are thrown to the nearest error boundary; the documented default throws when query.state.data is undefined.

Server rendering & testing::Error bounda.returns: A query whose failure can be propagated to the nearest React error boundary instead of being exposed only as query error state.

example.title: Throw a query error to an error boundary
example.explanation: Set throwOnError to true so a failed query reaches the nearest React error boundary instead of only exposing query error state.

useCases.title: Fail the screen when required data is unavailable
useCases.scenario: A page cannot render meaningful content without its initial query result.

useCases.title: Keep stale data visible during background failure
useCases.scenario: A query has previously loaded data and later fails during refetch.

useCases.title: Propagate mutation errors
useCases.scenario: A mutation failure should be handled by the same UI boundary as query failures.

interview.question: How do you send query failures to an error boundary?
interview.answer: Set throwOnError to true on the query. A failed query then propagates to the nearest React error boundary rather than remaining only in query error state.
interview.followUp: What is the default predicate? It throws when query.state.data is undefined, so background failures do not replace already available data.

interview.question: What does the default throwOnError behavior protect?
interview.answer: By default, errors are thrown only when there is no data to show. If the cache contains successfully fetched data, the component continues rendering even when that data is stale.
interview.followUp: How can every error be handled by a boundary? In non-configurable suspense behavior, manually throw the error after checking the error and fetching state.

interview.question: How are error boundaries reset for another attempt?
interview.answer: After an error, use QueryErrorResetBoundary or useQueryErrorResetBoundary to tell queries to retry when the component renders again. These APIs coordinate resetting query errors with the boundary retry flow.
interview.followUp: What does the hook scope cover? It resets query errors within the closest QueryErrorResetBoundary.

keyPoints: Suspense replaces query status and error handling with React Suspense and error boundaries.
Mutations can also use throwOnError: true to propagate failures to the nearest boundary.
The default query policy throws when the query has no cached data.
Use the boundary component or hook to reset query errors before retrying.
gotchas: The default does not throw every failure: if cached data exists, the query can continue rendering it.
With suspense, the default throw behavior cannot be changed; manually throw the error when all failures must reach the boundary.

Server rendering & testing::Hydration bo.summary: Hydration boundaries transfer prefetched TanStack Query data from server to client. Dehydrate the server cache, pass it through the loader, and provide it to HydrationBoundary to avoid an unnecessary initial client fetch.
Server rendering & testing::Hydration bo.explanation: A server-side QueryClient first prefetches the queries needed for rendering. Its cache is converted to serializable state with dehydrate, returned through the framework loader, and supplied to a client-side HydrationBoundary, which restores the state into the browser QueryClient so the initial render can use prefetched data instead of issuing a duplicate fetch.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: The serialized query-cache snapshot produced by dehydrate(queryClient) and supplied by the framework loader.

Server rendering & testing::Hydration bo.returns: The page subtree wrapped by HydrationBoundary is rendered with the transferred query cache restored on the client.

example.title: Prefetch, dehydrate, and hydrate
example.explanation: The server loader prefetches and dehydrates the cache; the rendered tree passes that state to HydrationBoundary so the client can reuse it.

useCases.scenario: A server-rendered route needs query data immediately on its first HTML render.

useCases.title: Loader-based prefetching
useCases.scenario: A framework loader can fetch route queries before rendering and expose serialized loader data to the client.

useCases.title: Multiple hydrated subtrees
useCases.scenario: A page contains independently rendered query-driven subtrees that can receive separate prefetched state.

interview.question: How does server rendering avoid refetching prefetched data on the client?
interview.answer: On the server, create a QueryClient, prefetch the required queries, and call dehydrate(queryClient). Return that state from the framework loader, then pass it to HydrationBoundary on the client. The boundary hydrates the cache so the browser can avoid a new initial fetch.
interview.followUp: Why is a per-request QueryClient preferable? It isolates one request's prefetched cache from another request and prevents cross-request data contamination.

interview.question: How should multiple server queries be prefetched efficiently?
interview.answer: The loader should prefetch every query needed for the rendered route before markup generation. Each query can be awaited explicitly, and independent queries should be started together with Promise.all when possible to reduce server-side latency.
interview.followUp: What changes when query dependencies are sequential? Start the dependent query only after its prerequisite data exists; parallelize only independent work.

interview.question: What is framework-specific in a hydration-boundary implementation?
interview.answer: The dehydrated state is not obtained through one universal API shape: frameworks differ in how loader data is returned and supplied to the rendered tree. The stable integration point is dehydrate on the server and HydrationBoundary state on the client.
interview.followUp: Can one application use more than one boundary? Yes, the advanced guidance documents multiple HydrationBoundary instances and separate dehydrated clients as valid patterns.

keyPoints: Prefetch route data before generating or rendering server markup.
Dehydration turns the server cache into state that can cross the server-to-browser boundary.
Client hydration restores the transferred state into the React Query cache.
A successfully hydrated prefetched query can supply the initial client data without an immediate duplicate request.
Create the QueryClient inside the framework loader used for the request.
Return the dehydrated cache from the loader so the framework can make it available to the client.
Place the rendered subtree inside HydrationBoundary and provide the loader's dehydrated state.
gotchas: Prefetch independent queries in parallel when the framework and data dependencies allow it, rather than awaiting each one sequentially.
The mechanism for obtaining the dehydrated state is framework-specific, so adapt the loader return syntax to the framework in use.

Server rendering & testing::Per-request.summary: Create a QueryClient within each server-rendering request or app lifecycle, never at module scope, to keep users' cached data isolated. Prefetch, dehydrate, and hydrate the cache to transfer server-fetched data to the browser.
Server rendering & testing::Per-request.explanation: During server rendering, construct QueryClient inside the request or application lifecycle rather than at module scope. Prefetch the required data, serialize the cache with dehydrate, and hydrate it into a client-side cache so the browser can reuse the server result without sharing cached data between users.

example.title: Per-request server client
example.explanation: The loader constructs a client for this request, prefetches the required query, and returns a dehydrated cache for framework-specific hydration.

useCases.title: Isolated SSR requests
useCases.scenario: A server-rendered route needs user-specific queries without risking cache leakage between visitors.

useCases.title: SSR hydration
useCases.scenario: A framework loader fetches route data before rendering and passes the cache to the browser.

useCases.title: Isolated test state
useCases.scenario: A test needs a clean query cache for each test case or isolated render.

interview.question: Why must a QueryClient be created per server request?
interview.answer: Create the QueryClient inside the application or request lifecycle, not as a module-level singleton. This prevents cached data from one user or request being exposed to another while still allowing one client instance throughout that component lifecycle.
interview.followUp: What is the server-rendering sequence? Prefetch the required queries, dehydrate the cache into serializable data, return it through the framework, and hydrate a browser cache.

interview.question: What are the main server-rendering steps before the browser receives HTML?
interview.answer: The server must prefetch data before generating the markup. After prefetching, dehydrate the query cache into a serializable form that can be embedded in the rendered response.
interview.followUp: How can multiple independent queries be prefetched efficiently? Start them in parallel with Promise.all when the framework loader allows it.

interview.question: What does dehydration and hydration accomplish?
interview.answer: The client hydrates the dehydrated state into its React Query cache, which avoids an unnecessary new client-side fetch for data already obtained on the server. The exact way the dehydrated value is returned depends on the framework.
interview.followUp: What must be preserved when transferring the state? It must remain serializable, and the client must hydrate it before relying on the prefetched cache.

keyPoints: Instantiate QueryClient inside the request-handling application lifecycle rather than at module scope.
A fresh server client isolates each request's cache from every other user's cache.
Prefetch queries before producing server-rendered markup so the initial response can include their results.
Dehydrate the populated cache into serializable state that can cross from server-rendered output to the browser.
Hydrate the transferred state into the browser cache to reuse server-fetched query data.
gotchas: Do not create the server QueryClient at module scope: that can share cached data across users and requests.
Dehydration alone is insufficient; the client must hydrate the serialized state to reuse the prefetched data.

Server rendering & testing::Suspense mod.summary: Suspense mode lets React render pending UI through a Suspense boundary instead of making the query component branch on status. Use suspense-specific hooks and handle failures with an error boundary.
Server rendering & testing::Suspense mod.explanation: Suspense mode moves pending-state rendering out of the query component. A suspense-specific hook suspends while data is unavailable, allowing React.Suspense to show its fallback; errors are handled through an error boundary. For server rendering, queries using this approach must be prefetched so the server and client hydrate consistently.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: The same query options as useQuery, except throwOnError, enabled, and placeholderData.

parameters.name: queryFn
parameters.description: A query function that returns the requested data; it cannot be skipToken.

Server rendering & testing::Suspense mod.returns: The suspense hooks return query data without requiring a pending-state branch; the component suspends until the data is available.

example.title: Render pending UI with Suspense
example.explanation: The query suspends while fetching, so the surrounding boundary displays its fallback until data is available.

Server rendering & testing::Testing quer.summary: Test TanStack Query code with a fresh QueryClient for every test and disable retries by default. This isolates caches and makes failure tests finish promptly.
Server rendering & testing::Testing quer.explanation: For each test, create a separate QueryClient and configure its query defaults with retry: false. Provide that client to the tested component or hook. This prevents cache sharing between tests and avoids the default retry delay when testing failures; an explicit retry option on a query still overrides the client default.
Server rendering & testing::Testing quer.syntax: new QueryClient({ defaultOptions: { queries: { retry: false } } })

useCases.title: Prevent cache leakage

keyPoints: Configure retry: false in the QueryClient defaults supplied to the provider.
Failing queries normally retry three times with backoff, which can make error tests time out.
A distinct QueryClient per test keeps query caches and test outcomes isolated.
A query-level retry option takes precedence over the client-wide default.
gotchas: Client defaults apply throughout the component tree, but they do not override an explicit retry setting on an individual query.
If a client is shared, clear it before every test and avoid parallel execution, or use a fresh client per test.
